publications.title: Delegate the Details: Flexible Assembly Constraint Authoring for Collaborative XR
publications.teaserAlt: VR view of four pipe parts staged on a wooden pallet. Solid blue lines run from the pallet to a brass flanged pipe and a T-pipe, dashed orange lines run to a gray pipe and a valve, and a controller points at the gray pipe, which sits inside a glowing orange hull.
publications.teaserCaption: Parts staged on a pallet in VR, where solid blue links mark prescribed poses, dashed orange links mark delegated ones, and pointing at the gray pipe shows its bounding hull.

publications.title: Augmenting Human Performance with an XR Agent Learning from Online Behavior and BCI Evidence
publications.teaserAlt: Two panels of a diagram. Left, labeled b: evidence-quality sliders feed an online EM loop between a foundational VLM and a virtual prompt, above a grid of drone images marked red or blue. Right, labeled c: a person in a headset aims a controller among floating drones while red outlines and red curved lines mark targets, under a box that reads Agent provides task cues.

publications.title: Fast Digitization in XR of Reality-Linked Gaussian-Splatted Proxies
publications.teaserAlt: Headset passthrough view of a lab desk. Gaussian-splatted proxies of a spray bottle, a bag and a laptop float in pink wireframe boxes above the real bag, bottles and laptop on the desk.
publications.teaserCaption: Proxies of a spray bottle, a bag and a laptop, reconstructed by feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting, float in boxes above the desk. Each can be grabbed, inspected and used to select the physical object it came from.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: Lego assemblies on a desk, seen through the headset.
publications.videoCaption: Live capture and use of proxies on a Quest 3, with no cuts
publications.abstract: Capturing real objects as interactive 3D assets in XR typically requires offline photogrammetry. We present Gaussian-Splatted Proxies, a system for fast object digitization in XR using feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting. With a Quest 3 headset, users select objects detected by the system through the passthrough cameras, then capture images that an edge server reconstructs as interactive Gaussian splats. Our system extracts individual objects from scene reconstructions without any per-scene training by projecting detection bounding boxes into 3D space. The resulting assets can be grabbed, inspected, rotated, and used to select the corresponding objects in the physical world.

publications.title: Bimanual XR Specification of Relative and Absolute Assembly Hierarchies for Teleoperation
publications.teaserAlt: VR view of two nested hulls above a floor grid. A blue wireframe hull around a red shaft with two cyan gears sits inside a translucent orange hull, which also holds a pink gear on a green shaft.
publications.teaserCaption: An absolute group, drawn as a blue wireframe hull, nested inside a relative group, drawn as an orange hull. The robot chooses where to build a relative group, while an absolute group keeps the pose the author gives it within its parent.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: a gear and a group of parts inside nested hulls, with two controllers below.
publications.videoCaption: Grouping parts, nesting groups and switching between relative and absolute constraints, in VR
publications.abstract: We present a bimanual XR interaction approach for specifying remote assembly tasks as hierarchies of relative and absolute object constraints that specify high-level teleoperation goals for robots. Grabbing one object in each hand creates a constraint group (visualized as a hull) and groups can be nested into hierarchies. Each group can be relative (with a robot-specifiable 6DoF pose) or absolute (with an author-specified fixed 6DoF pose) in relation to its parent. A relative group specifies a subassembly that can be constructed at a location chosen by the robot software for efficiency rather than mandated by the user.

publications.title: Virtual Reality Task Guidance Through Relative 6DoF Pose Specification
publications.teaserAlt: VR scene with three groups of motor parts, each in its own translucent blue hull: two orange shell parts and two screws at upper left, two yellow frame parts at lower left, and the assembled inner chassis, a red ring around a gray disk, at right.
publications.teaserCaption: The orange shell parts, the yellow frame parts and the assembled inner chassis of a motor, each set enclosed in a translucent hull. Poses are specified only within each set, so a set can be placed anywhere.
publications.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) systems for guiding remote physical tasks typically require object poses to be specified in absolute world coordinates. However, many of these tasks only need object poses to be specified relative to each other. Thus, supporting only absolute pose specification can create inefficiencies in giving or following task guidance when unnecessary constraints are imposed. We are developing a VR task-guidance system that avoids this by enabling relative 6DoF poses to be specified within subsets of objects. We describe our user interface, including how geometric relationships are specified and several ways in which they are visualized, and our plans for validating our approach against existing techniques.

publications.title: Permanent Proxies for Bimanual Selection and Manipulation in VR
publications.teaserAlt: VR view over a wooden table. The left controller holds a motherboard proxy outlined in yellow, joined by a yellow arc to the original motherboard on the table. The right controller holds a RAM proxy outlined in red, joined by a red arc to the original RAM module, and a red outline on the motherboard proxy marks where the RAM goes.
publications.teaserCaption: Proxies of a motherboard and a RAM module, pulled into the hands and joined to their originals by arcs, with the RAM’s target pose outlined in red on the motherboard proxy. Manipulating a proxy moves its original, as in the Voodoo Dolls technique.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: a motherboard and its proxy on a table, joined by a red curve.
publications.videoCaption: The Voodoo Dolls technique, the two study conditions and the results
publications.abstract: Copies (proxies) of objects are useful for selecting and manipulating objects in virtual reality (VR). Temporary proxies are destroyed after use and must be recreated for reuse. Permanent proxies persist after use for easy reselection, but can cause clutter. To investigate the benefits and drawbacks of permanent and temporary proxies, we conducted a user study in which participants performed 6DoF tasks with proxies in the Voodoo Dolls technique, revealing that permanent proxies were more efficient for hard reselection and preferred.

publications.title: An XR GUI for Visualizing Messages in ECS Architectures
publications.teaserAlt: Headset view of a city street crossing. Nearby traffic lights are outlined in orange and farther ones in bluish green, red arrowheads run along the links between them, blue arrowheads mark messages in transit, and the right controller is outlined in yellow.
publications.teaserCaption: Entities in a street scene are outlined by how far a message has propagated, yellow for the right controller, then orange and bluish green for successive sets of traffic lights. Red arrowheads trace the links, and blue arrowheads are messages traveling along them.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: a city street with a traffic light, seen from the headset with tracked hands.
publications.videoCaption: The XR GUI in a street scene, alongside the developer working in the Unity editor
publications.abstract: Entity--Component--System (ECS) architectures are fundamental to many systems for developing extended reality (XR) applications. These applications often contain complex scenes and require intricately connected application logic to connect components together, making debugging and analysis difficult. Graph-based tools have been created to show actions in ECS-based scene hierarchies, but few address interactions that go beyond traditional hierarchical communication. To address this, we present an XR GUI for Mercury (a toolkit to handle cross-component ECS communication) that allows developers to view and edit relationships and interactions between scene entities in Mercury.

publications.title: SwEYEpinch and Beyond: Exploring Intuitive, Efficient Text Entry for Extended Reality via Eye and Hand Tracking
publications.teaserAlt: Drawing of a virtual keyboard. An eye icon moves from the t key to the o key while a hand holds a pinch, and word suggestions sit above the keys.
publications.teaserCaption: Gaze swipes across the keys while the hand holds a pinch, and suggestions appear before the swipe ends. Cropped from the paper’s teaser figure.
publications.abstract: Despite steady progress, text entry in Extended Reality (XR) often remains slower and more effortful than typing on a physical keyboard or touchscreen. We explore a simple idea: use gaze to swipe through a virtual keyboard for the fast, low-effort where and a manual pinch held throughout the swipe for the when, extending and validating it through a series of user studies. We first show that a basic version including a low-latency decoder with spatiotemporal Dynamic Time Warping and fixation filtering outperforms selecting individual keys sequentially, either by finger tapping each or gazing at each while pinching. We then add mid-swipe prediction and in-gesture cancellation, improving words per minute (WPM) without hurting accuracy. We show that this approach is faster and more preferred than previous gaze-swipe approaches, finger tapping with prediction, or hand swiping with the same additions. Furthermore, a seven-day, 30-session study demonstrates sustained learning, with peak performance reaching 64.7 WPM.

publications.title: VHard: An XR UI for Kinesthetic Rehearsal of Rock Climbing Moves
publications.teaserAlt: Two views of one grip. Left, a photo of a hand gripping a white climbing hold. Right, the same grip in VHard, where a translucent hand closes on the scanned hold and the hold is highlighted green where the hand touches it.
publications.teaserCaption: A hand gripping the physical H10 hold of a MoonBoard, and the same grip in VHard, where the scanned hold is highlighted green to show where it is gripped.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: a translucent hand on a green hold among scanned holds.
publications.videoCaption: Rehearsing moves in XR, alongside footage of the same climbs on a real MoonBoard
publications.abstract: Rock climbers frequently struggle to complete climbs due to the difficulty of practicing precise movements without actually attempting them. A standard strategy is to kinesthetically rehearse the hand and body positions required while on the ground. However, the lack of live feedback severely hampers this method because climbers can only roughly estimate the distances and positions involved. We introduce VHard, an extended reality (XR) application that visualizes the precision and accuracy of hand placements on a metric digital twin of a MoonBoard climbing wall. VHard augments kinesthetic rehearsal with XR feedback in order to assist climbers in completing difficult boulder problems.

publications.title: Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality for Ice-Sheet Data Analysis
publications.teaserAlt: XR view of ice-penetrating radar cross-sections standing as vertical panels above a terrain surface, with a data panel at right.
publications.teaserCaption: Ice-penetrating radar cross-sections stand as vertical panels in 3D above the terrain, where they can be inspected and interpreted.
publications.videoAlt: Still from the video: a presenter beside a large video wall showing radar data in 3D.
publications.videoCaption: A live demonstration of the application on a stage video wall
publications.abstract: Three-dimensional geospatial thinking is an important skillset used by earth scientists and students to analyze and interpret data [1]. This method of inquiry is useful in glaciology, where traditional geophysical survey techniques have been adapted to map three-dimensional (3D) ice sheet structures and inform studies of ice flow, mass change, and history in both Greenland and Antarctica. Ice-penetrating radar images the ice in two-dimensional (2D) cross-sections from the surface to the base. Analysis of this data often requires visual inspection and 3D interpretation, but is hindered by data visualization tools and techniques that rarely transcend the two-dimensionality of the computer screen [2]. Recent advances in Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR), together referred to as Extended Reality (XR), offer a glimpse into the future of 3D ice-sheet data analysis [3]. These technologies offer users an immersive experience where 3D geospatial datasets can be understood more immediately than with 2D maps, and gestural user interfaces can enhance understanding. Here we present Pol-XR, an XR application that supports both visualization and interpretation of ice-penetrating radar in Antarctica and Greenland.

preprints.title: PointGrade: Geometric Priors for Grading MoonBoard Problems
preprints.teaserAlt: Left part of a pipeline diagram. A MoonBoard problem goes to BetaMove, which outputs an ordered sequence of moves. A photo of a prescanned MoonBoard leads to a copy that shows only the problem’s holds in red, labeled sample point cloud of holds in problem, which feeds PointNet++, drawn with its network diagram, and a 1024-dimensional feature vector.
preprints.teaserCaption: The input side of the pipeline: BetaMove orders a MoonBoard problem’s moves, and the problem’s holds, shown in red, are sampled as a point cloud from a prescanned board for PointNet++.
preprints.abstract: A MoonBoard is a standardized bouldering wall used in gyms around the world. Climbs up the wall limited to only a subset of holds are known as problems. We introduce PointGrade, a novel machine learning approach to predicting the difficulty of a MoonBoard problem. By sampling a point cloud from pre-scanned meshes of every hold, our model combines 3D object classification architecture with existing sequence-based approaches to difficulty grade prediction. Our method captures latent geometric information contained the climb, outperforming other work on the problem that neglect this data.
